Richard: Well, we’ll take a walk through the paper-machine buildings. Basically, my time’s your time, so whatever you wanna see. If you— Brooks: Before the explosion, the mill ran 24/7. From town, you could hear it, and sometimes Jay would reek of sulfur. Inside the mill were dozens of workers—mechanics, electricians, maintenance workers, and operators. Richard: When we were up and running, it would be nothing for it to be, like, 95 or so degrees up here. Yeah. We’d be sweating. You wouldn’t be able to hear me talk. I wouldn’t be able to hear you talk. We’d be hollering at each other. Summer, you’d go outside to cool off. Brooks: Now it’s deathly quiet. Walking around in the mill, it was immediately clear why Elon Musk wants to put data centers in outer space. The paper-machine rooms are dark and cold and seem endless. Brooks: Did it look much different before demolition down here? Richard: Oh, yeah. So this kind of looks— Brooks: But there were still signs of what the place used to be. Lucien pointed out a mural on one of the walls, a wooden boat full of puppies looking out at a row of ducklings. Brooks: Where’d this mural come from? Richard: We had some pretty talented people that used to work here. [ Music ] Brooks: The case for the project in Jay rests on the existing infrastructure of the mill. The reason the Trump administration is pushing to convert brownfield sites for data-center use is because operating industrial machinery requires immense power, as does operating a data center. According to the developer, the site is already allowed to pull a lot of power from the electric grid. He plans to add solar panels and use the hydroelectric power that’s already on site. Elsewhere in the country, power plants are struggling to keep up with demand from data centers. The cost of electricity, especially in areas near data centers, is super high—high enough to become a serious election issue this year, and high enough for Google, Microsoft, and Open AI to sign a pledge this spring to keep costs down for everyone else. The pitch, then, is that the project in Jay will exist in a kind of walled garden—it would generate much of its power on-site and pull no more from the grid than the mill did just a few years before the explosion. The argument for water use runs along the same lines: Especially in states like Arizona, data centers strain the water supply in a state that is very dry. Maine is wet. Richard: So basically, these are the pumps that would pump water from the river up to the mill. Brooks: Lucien showed me the water-treatment plant on site, another vast room. The paper mill used to use about 35 million gallons of water from the river per day. The developer says the data center would use 1 percent of that. Lucien wondered out loud if they might need a smaller pump. These numbers, they come from the developer. He is from Maine, by the way. His client is called Sentinel. They’re one of the big companies in the data-center construction world. And it’s important to say: There’s a high degree of uncertainty in this proposal. Some of the language used by the developer—like there would be, quote, “no environmental impact” and, quote, “The project is all positives and has no negatives”—is plainly false. Much of the rest of it is just unknown. Maine has environmental and power regulations like everywhere else, but no specific playbook for data centers. The reason the Maine legislature—Republicans and Democrats—passed the moratorium in the first place was so they could make a set of rules before development starts. A data center in Jay might end up looking like what the developer is pitching. Or it might look very different. Richard: The concern people have about electricity and water, I understand it for, let’s say, downtown Lewiston, Farmington, Bangor. They don’t have the infrastructure set up. This place is gonna operate, could operate, all on its own. Brooks: The mill, or its absence, seems to be the reason why Jay is willing to accept a level of uncertainty that other towns are not. On every point, this is how the argument goes: A data center can’t be as loud as the mill, can’t smell as bad as the mill, can’t pollute like the mill . Richard: It’s the perfect fit. You need lots of water. We used to use lots and lots of water. You need lots of power. We used to use or make lots of power. It’s a natural fit. All you gotta do is get over the people’s fear. Brooks: Using the past in this way, as a means of justifying the future, it’s an imperfect science, especially with the layer of nostalgia covering everything. For Katlin, on her farm, this sort of argument just doesn’t make sense. The present, without a mill or a data center, is clearly better for the environment than the past. On the other hand, the mill has been closed for six years. Jay needs something. The mill is a handy benchmark for what they’re willing to tolerate. Richard: Let me just get out of it. You want the light on or off? [ Music ] Brooks: When I was touring the mill with Lucien, the thing that stuck with me was that mural he showed me—the boat full of puppies. The developer’s plan is to clear the space until it’s empty, and then some trucks will roll up, servers will be plugged in, and the building will start humming. If all goes well with the plan to turn this mill into a data center, that mural will be a sort of cave painting one day. Maybe some AI-powered robot will roll past and wonder what possible efficiency might have been gained by painting a boat full of puppies on a wall in a workplace. In 2020, when the pulp mill exploded in Jay, over 500 people worked there. Not long after, it was zero. That’s a shock that’s hard to measure in a town of about 5,000. For Cody, it meant that his plan to work his way up at the mill, fund the 401(k), and live a life that looked a lot like his grandfather’s wasn’t going to happen. Brooks: I mean, you were saying earlier that it felt like a stable thing, a career, a job you could have for a while. Jacques: Yeah. It was stable. I could picture, you know—I was training for the next job, you know. I was gonna get the big raise, blah, blah, blah. To, all of a sudden, now, you know, what the heck are we gonna do here? [ Door opens ] Trevor Doiron: Hi. How are you? Brooks: When I visited Jay, I spent an afternoon with Trevor Doiron. Doiron: I’m running for state House here in Jay. Neighbor: This neighborhood is full of Doirons. Brooks: Trevor was a few years below Cody at Spruce Mountain High School. He’s 28 years old, and he’s running as a Democrat to represent Jay’s district in the state House. He supports the data-center project. Doiron: Well, I grew up right the next street over. Brooks: When Trevor is out campaigning, when people open their doors to talk to him, what he sees worries him. Doiron: I’ve seen some pretty scary things. I mean, people living with holes in the floor, using the stove to heat the house, people doing their best to get by but putting themselves in grave danger because there’s no good jobs; there’s no way to earn a really honest income. Brooks: The town itself is now the second largest employer in Jay, behind the high school. The third largest is Hannaford, a grocery store. Maine has the oldest population in the country. Jay is older than the average in Maine. Doiron: Like, a lot of the services for the elderly, it’s like, the elderly are the ones providing the services for other elderly people. We’ve got the food pantry over here. We got a guy; he’s great—92 years old, and he goes every Tuesday. [ Music ] Doiron: Fills the boxes. But he’s not gonna be able to do that forever. Like a year from now, who’s gonna be filling the boxes at the food pantry? Who’s gonna be delivering the meals to the seniors who can’t get out and do their shopping or cook for themselves? It kinda feels like a silent sense of resignation. Brooks: This, then, was my best theory as to why Jay fought for its data center: desperation. The town needs something, anything , to stay afloat. After the mill closed, Cody and his girlfriend had their first kid, a daughter. Cody needed to work, needed to provide for his family. He heard from a friend that if you could get in as a union electrician, there was work and the pay was good. He took an aptitude test, became an apprentice, and before too long, he had a new career. Jacques: Went up to camp with the family for Labor Day weekend, and then I got in my truck and drove down to Niagara Falls because they had this job that was called Lake Mariner data center, and I had no idea what a data center was. I just knew that it was a good opportunity. Brooks: Cody, a few short years after the mill closed, made a new career as an electrician working in data centers. Jacques: So I really had no electrical background. Just worked at the paper mill and kinda knew that I didn’t want a place to just blow up on me and next thing I know, I lose my job. Brooks: The debate around data centers around the country often comes back to jobs. Maine’s governor cited jobs as a central reason for her veto of the moratorium. Ad: I grew up here, and I wanted my kids to be able to do the same. Brooks: Meta recently spent $6 million on an ad campaign linking data centers and jobs. Ad: We’re bringing jobs home. Brooks: Specifically, Meta is talking about full-time, long-term jobs. Ad: For us, and for our next generation. Brooks: I figured the promise of these full-time jobs was central in the town’s support for its data-center project, especially with the sudden loss of the mill. When I asked Tom Saviello, the county commissioner, it seemed like his ambitions went well beyond jobs. Tom Saviello: You build that, and they will come, just like Field of Dreams . We need technology to change this place and how we operate. And if this is our opportunity to jump on that technology, let’s ride the horse, and then give us a chance to figure out: What do we do next? I can see something here. I can’t tell you what it is. Brooks: The developer has said he expects the data center will employ 125 to 150 people full-time. He also says there will be 800 to 1,000 temporary construction jobs to get the data center up and running. But the evidence so far does not look good for those long-term jobs. A data center of the size being proposed in Jay might only employ 30 to 50 full-time staff. And who knows what those jobs will look like in the future. Given all the Field of Dreams talk, I figured Tom had high hopes for these jobs. But as we spoke more, I heard something else. Saviello: I don’t care if it’s 10 jobs. I don’t care if it’s 100 jobs. We used to employ, when I got here, 1,000 workers—good salaries, good benefits. There aren’t very many employed now. So even one is more than zero. Brooks: Over and over, I heard a version of this—not some vision of Jay returned to its former glory, but humbly, The mill is a big place. It’s just sitting there. It should be something . Richard: I mean, look at the space. If you can put something in here, why wouldn’t you? It’s here. McLeod: I loved that place. I’m the person that goes to work every day happy ’cause I love my job. So to see it be a shell of nothing, you want something there. Jay wouldn’t be Jay without the paper mill that we had. You know, you don’t wanna see Jay just be nothing. Brooks: I had this idea that to survive, Jay needed anything. But what I heard in these conversations was different. First of all, there’s a positivity on AI that I didn’t quite expect. Vicki is excited about what it might do in medicine. Cody mused about how it might help with his daughter’s education. And second, a lot of the people I spoke with wanted to get in the weeds with me on energy infrastructure. In interview after interview, they talked to me about cooling systems, hydroelectric dams, water tables, and retention ponds, and decibel limits. McLeod: Maybe we understand the workings of the industry and know that it’s gotta come from somewhere. It’s not magic. I mean, it’s like electricity. It’s not magic, you know? Brooks: Yeah. McLeod: Somehow it’s gotta be made. You might not like solar, you might not like wind, you might not like water, you might not like nuclear, but you like power. So it’s just like, I don’t love solar fields, but I love electricity . Brooks: Mm-hmm. McLeod: I don’t love wind farms, but I love electricity . Brooks: For Jay, the question wasn’t so much “Why should we have a data center here?” It was “Why shouldn’t we?” [ Music ] Brooks: This moment, the rapid-fire building of the infrastructure for AI, is one of the largest capital expenditures in human history. In many places, that means destroying farmland, polluting, and putting immense pressure on the grid— sometimes achieved through secrecy, pressure, and manipulation. Other times, towns offer incentives. In a recent article about Jay and rural data centers, Anthony Elmo, who studies economic development, said of rural towns: “They don’t have the resources to negotiate. They don’t know what to ask for. They don’t have the legal expertise, and they don’t feel like they have the leverage.” I think Jays knows plenty. The town offered no tax break and stood to make about $6 million in property taxes, something like three-quarters of the town budget. When I asked what might come of such a massive windfall, Trevor Doiron told me he didn’t know—that would be up to the people of Jay. When they talked about jobs, no one had any notion of appearing in a Meta ad. They said one is better than zero and reminded me that “temporary construction jobs” are full-time work to union electricians like Cody. Brooks: In an earlier era, his dad’s generation even, Cody wouldn’t have to choose between a good salary and being with his family. But now he does. Jacques: I’ve been given this opportunity, so I feel like I’m gonna kinda seize that opportunity, you know. These companies are just paying massive amounts of money, and I’d be a fool not to chase it. Brooks: Cody drives all over the country, most recently about eight hours to Niagara Falls, and stays on the job for weeks at a time. Jacques: This Lake Mariner data center is being funded and backed by Google. They know guys like me and guys like other guys in the country are gonna come to chase that money. These tech companies have the money to pay us accordingly, and sometimes we can get them to do it. Brooks: When he’s traveling for a job, Cody lives in an Airbnb with a bunch of other electricians, also traveling, also chasing data-center money away from home. At the mill, Cody told me work felt like being in a family. They made meals together, spent holidays together, and then, he went home to his actual family. Cody’s new life, though, it’s a sort of exchange. He spends more time with his union brothers, who live all over the country, than he spends with his actual brother, who works in a restaurant near Jay. He does this so he can send money home for his girlfriend and their 4-year-old daughter. [ Music ] Brooks: Recently, Cody was working six or seven days a week. Somehow, the project was already behind schedule, which meant he wouldn’t have time to go home. Jacques: I was working at the data center, and it was gonna be about eight weeks that I was gonna be gone from home, and after about the fourth week, I really was just getting homesick. You know, I wouldn’t call it despair, but you’re like, All right, I really just miss what’s familiar to me . So I pretty much told them, like, “I’m not gonna make eight weeks without seeing you guys.” Brooks: So Cody and his girlfriend made a plan. She was in Jay. He was in Niagara Falls. Albany was halfway, so they decided to meet there just for a day. Jacques: I beat them to the hotel, and I remember my girlfriend and daughter pulling up, you know. My girlfriend rolled my daughter’s window down. I just remember kind of being elated to see them, you know, just kind of like a sigh of relief, just grab them and hug them and kind of forget about everything else for a few minutes there, and it’s just good to kind of be around them. [ Music ] Jacques: We spent 24 hours together, and then, you know, my girlfriend and daughter got back in the car and drove to Maine, and I got back in my truck and drove back to Niagara Falls. We’re a young family. I just bought a house. I’m putting an addition on my house. I’m trying to build a garage. Working a job, unfortunately, in Jay, Maine, you’re not having a new truck, a tractor, a snowmobile. You know, you’re not necessarily living the American dream that we grew up hearing about. Brooks: What’s exciting for Cody is that a data center in Maine might mean Jay could have the best of both worlds. Saviello: They deserve it here. They’ve been through turmoil, whether it be the blow-up or whether it be the shutdown. It’s been turmoil here, but they’ve survived. And this has got a chance for them to even do better. Like I said, in Field of Dreams , “Build it, and they will come.” People will be working, and the town will prosper. [ Music ] Brooks: On June 11, less than a month after I visited, the town of Jay posted to its Facebook page with commenting disabled. The data-center project had been put on indefinite hold because the company behind it, Sentinel, had backed out. I called a lot of the people I spoke to when I was there. Most were disappointed, and most weren’t totally surprised. The data center was just the latest on a long list of things that were there one day and gone the next. [ Music ] Brooks: This episode of Radio Atlantic was edited by Theo Balcomb. Production help Jacob Smollen. Fact-checking by Yvonne Kim. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. I’m Ethan Brooks. Thanks for listening.

items.title: Iran’s War Within
items.description: For the past few months, Iran has intermittently fought a war with the United States, Israel, and its Arab neighbors. But throughout this period, it has never stopped waging war on its own citizens. The Islamic Republic is executing Iranians in record numbers and has sharpened its tools of repression. Such tactics have never succeeded in pacifying Iranian society for long. Today, some civil-society leaders, and even figures inside the establishment itself, fret that the regime’s heavy domestic hand is not only hurting Iranians but also weakening the country’s war effort. On Tuesday, the Iranian regime executed two young men. Abolfazl Sepahi, 23, and Amirhossein Safari, 28, had been arrested in Isfahan in January in connection with the nationwide anti-regime protests. Dozens of Isfahanis came out to protest the two men’s execution in the days leading up to it, but to no avail. On Monday, security forces dispersed the crowd with paintballs, tear gas, and shots into the air. Sepahi and Safari were hanged in the very same square where they had allegedly demonstrated. Back in January, the regime put down mammoth protests with particular brutality, killing thousands of people in the space of two days. In the months since, Iranian courts have sentenced dozens of citizens to death for taking part in the protests. According to UN estimates, 24 have already been executed. According to Amnesty International, at least 60 others, including some who were arrested as children, remain at risk of execution. [ Read: The war that shall not be named ] Sepahi and Safari were among 60 people accused of killing four members of the police forces during the protests in Isfahan. The regime claims that the four officers were tied up in the city’s central square, stoned, and then burned alive. Earlier this month, two other young men—a 19-year-old Iranian and a 24-year-old Afghan national—were executed in connection with the same events, and a dozen more people face capital punishment for them. The regime media have distributed an unclear video from the incident and aired confessions of some of the arrestees. But no due process was available to the accused, and the regime media are known for airing forced confessions. Sepahi and Safari had access to no legal representation, not even court-appointed lawyers. They were reportedly tried in three virtual court sessions, each of which took about an hour and in which the accused phoned in from prison rather than appearing before the judge. Among those alarmed by the state’s mounting repression are civil-society figures who have staunchly opposed the war with America and Israel. Emadeddin Baghi, an Iranian human-rights activist who is nevertheless not an advocate of regime change, expressed shock about the handling of the Isfahan cases on an Iranian podcast. He said that he had been trying to assist with the defense for one of the accused, but before the person could even start an appeals process, he was executed. The judiciary’s heavy hand will make citizens “question the regime” and will lead to a “fall of credibility and legitimacy, resulting in unhappiness, anger, and violence,” Baghi cautioned. Likewise, on Tuesday, a group of 150 civic and political activists published a statement calling on the regime to free political prisoners and stop the executions. The signatories include activists such as Abdollah Momeni and Alireza Rajayi, who both oppose what they term “foreign aggression” against Iran and also call for a referendum to change the country’s constitution. They see the regime’s repression as weakening the country at a time of war. Executions are not the regime’s only coercive instrument. Many professors at Iranian universities have been suspended or violently arrested, according to the Toronto-based Association of Iranian Studies. And other signs suggest that the regime is clamping down on public life. Iran’s hijab laws, mandating that women cover their hair and body, have been laxly enforced since 2024, including during the war. “Even at the airports, you can now see most people without hijab,” a woman who asked to be called Elmira, 27, told me. Like others I spoke with, she used an alias for her safety. “Since it’s summer, I go around mostly with a top and without covering my hair or shoulders, and I have never been stopped once this summer.” But last week, the police clamped down on Tehran’s Sanayi Avenue, a popular destination for nightlife and street culture. At least seven cafés were shut down; their owners were told that they could reopen only if they refused to serve hijabless women. The authorities also destroyed public benches that had become hangout spots. “The benches were where you could bring your coffee, smoke a little, have some social life in the midst of the damn war,” Maryam, 32, told me. “But now that’s gone. They don’t want us to breathe.” A workspace-sharing business in Tehran’s Book Garden, a cultural complex, was also forced to close , casting 270 workers into unemployment. Other cities, including Mashhad and Qom, have seen a crackdown on public spaces as well. In Rasht, a particularly liberal city close to the Caspian coast, police have started accosting women on the streets and threatening them with arrest if they refuse the hijab. There, too, cafés have been pressured to refuse to serve uncovered women, a young woman who recently traveled there told me. [ Graeme Wood: The U.S. is subtly shifting its Iran strategy ] Iran’s social policy is a divisive subject in national-security circles. Some inside the ruling establishment have been pushing for the draconian enforcement of the Islamic dress code. Hamshahri , a newspaper controlled by Tehran’s hard-line mayor, Alireza Zakani, recently asked the police and judiciary to punish hijab-less women for their “bad appearances” and “norm violations,” contending that such women represented an “organized project” of “cultural shamelessness.” Some members of Parliament and regional officials have made similar calls in recent weeks. More pragmatic figures in the establishment accuse these hard-liners of upsetting the country’s social peace with needless political repression, and by seeking to micromanage the lifestyles of ordinary people. They accuse the hard-liners of doing the bidding of Iran’s adversaries, the United States and Israel, by causing instability that will ultimately hurt the regime. Even in these dark times, Iran still roils with unrest. Shopkeepers in bazaars have staged sit-ins, not unlike those that preceded the January protests. And just in the past few days, farmers have protested for lack of water, residents of Zanjan have demonstrated for housing, oil and gas employees have rallied in several facilities in the south, and several prisons, including one in Rasht, have become flash points for crowds registering their opposition to the continued executions. Having fought off several rounds of nationwide protests since 2017, the Iranian regime knows full well that many of its citizens detest it. The response it reaches for is always the same: repression, which has never yet produced social peace. As the Islamic Republic seeks to manage its military conflict with the United States, it will likely find that the home front remains the hardest to win.

items.title: Abdul El-Sayed Fuses Together Two Toxic Ideologies
items.description: Abdul El-Sayed is running for Senate as a Democrat in Michigan, where he is waging a close and bitter contest against Representative Haley Stevens in a primary that will be held on Tuesday. Were he to win, and then go on to defeat Mike Rogers, the presumed Republican candidate, El-Sayed would become the most fervently anti-Zionist senator. “If you want your politics dictated to you by AIPAC or Chuck Schumer, then I’m not your guy,” he said during a debate with Stevens. El-Sayed depicts Israel and its American supporters as the primary authors of Donald Trump’s foreign policy. He also blames Israel and AIPAC for a wide array of domestic social problems. “We should be using our tax dollars here to invest in health care here and education here, rather than sending it over there to buy bombs and tanks that get used to drive apartheid and genocide there,” he said to WDET, Detroit’s public-radio station. El-Sayed has barely acknowledged the possibility that Stevens is a sentient being with individual agency, describing her as “a suit with a large AIPAC bank account.” Asked recently on CNN if he thought there were any reasons other than money that someone might have a different view on Israel, he said, “Not if you’re a Democrat and you believe in human rights.” Asked if a progressive could also be a Zionist, he replied, “Every definition of a Jewish state ends up in some articulation of illiberal values, every single one.” The magnitude of the shift in Democratic politics that El-Sayed’s election would create has not quite registered with the party’s voters. In part this is because New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, also a fervent anti-Zionist, attracted so much attention and controversy in his campaign last year that El-Sayed’s run feels like a tamer sequel. In reality, however, not only was Mamdani running in a far different locale (an overwhelmingly Democratic city rather than a purple state), but he also, with rare exceptions, focused on affordability, not on Israel. It was his opponents who sounded obsessed with Israel. [ Listen: A battle for the future of the Democratic Party ] El-Sayed’s campaign is currently the left’s preeminent cause, held up as key proof that an obsessively anti-Zionist left-wing politics can win outside of blue enclaves. Michigan voted twice for Donald Trump. Should El-Sayed prevail, he would immediately open the door for a new wave of like-minded candidates to follow behind him. “You put one ogre on a pike,” El-Sayed told donors in a Zoom call, according to Politico , apparently referring to Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, “and then everyone else gets the message, and all of a sudden starts to sound a lot different.” But if El-Sayed’s anti-Zionism is obsessive, it is not a singular obsession. He talks about the Israel lobby the way he talks on the stump about nearly any other political issue. The El-Sayed formula is to describe just about any policy as a conspiracy by a corporate entity or wealthy cabal to enrich itself at the expense of the people. The villains in his stories are motivated by pure greed, and trade-offs do not exist. This is a rhetorical style that has long existed on the populist left. The trouble is that, when you apply it to the Israel-Palestine conflict, and especially to the question of why some Americans do not share El-Sayed’s position on it, his approach grows paranoid and menacing. Populists believe, almost as an article of faith, that Democrats can win working-class voters by moving left on economic policy. El-Sayed has aligned himself with the Democratic Party’s Bernie Sanders–and–Elizabeth Warren wing, endorsing Medicare for All, promising to end Citizens United, supporting targeted tariffs, emphasizing the evils of corporate monopolies , and generally making the answer to every political question a blunt attack on billionaire greed. When applied to ordinary problems, this rhetorical mode yields oversimplistic but crowd-pleasing answers. “Why don’t our schools get the funding that they deserve? Well, because there’s not a lobby for schools. Kids don’t have a corporate PAC,” El-Sayed says , in a typical piece of campaign rhetoric. In truth, there is a powerful lobby for school funding: teachers’ unions. The main barrier to more spending on schools is not the absence of lobbying; it’s that people don’t like paying taxes. After Gretchen Whitmer, the state’s popular Democratic governor, endorsed Stevens last week, El-Sayed explained the choice as the inevitable product of the two women’s benefactors. “Those who have taken corporate money for most of their careers tend to stick together,” he said. When this populist analysis is extended to Israel, it takes on an even more conspiratorial edge. El-Sayed’s efforts to weave a seamless narrative connecting AIPAC to his struggle against wealthy interests has built the Israel lobby into an almost-supernatural force controlling American politics behind the scenes. Graham Platner—who was running competitively in polls against Susan Collins, the Republican senator from Maine, before scandals overtook him—preceded El-Sayed as the movement’s cause célèbre. He similarly depicted himself as the tribune of the people fighting a twilight struggle against oligarchs. When reporters began to unearth evidence of questionable behavior, his supporters quickly concluded that his twin struggles against oligarchy and Zionism—perhaps it was a single struggle—had made him a target. “The thing about this smear campaign is that it’s obvious,” wrote the American Economic Liberties Project researcher Matt Stoller on X. “Graham Platner wants to eliminate the power of billionaires, and wants to end our alliance with Israel. That’s all these slurs are about, not what he did or who he is.” The podcaster Krystal Ball posited a “clear double standard at play with Platner reporting because he is anti-zionist and anti-oligarch.” Sam Haselby, a historian and an author, wrote on X, “Let’s be serious. They don’t like Platner because he’s an economic populist. They have no trouble with vastly worse sexual ethics as long as one is pro-billionaire and pro Israel.” The basis for these charges is a bit cracked. But it follows logically from the populist analysis of the situation. If all resistance that left-wing candidates face is the work of a shadowy moneyed interest, and fighting Israel is the left’s most deeply felt cause, then it stands to reason that Israel, or its lobbyists, are behind every setback the movement encounters. Earlier this month, El-Sayed casually dismissed a poll showing Stevens leading him by a point by telling MS NOW, “That poll seems to be funded by AIPAC,” which is not true . Pro-Israel lobbying does play an important role in domestic politics, and it does often include spurious charges of anti-Semitism to discredit legitimate critiques of Israel. Aid to Israel is not, however, a meaningful constraint on American domestic spending, given that aid to Israel accounts for less than one tenth of 1 percent of the federal budget. The populists are not imagining that they are fighting a well-funded lobby. What they are imagining is that this lobby is the hidden force behind all of the opposition they face. I received a small taste of this political style earlier this spring, when I wrote an article criticizing El-Sayed’s claim that he can adopt unpopular left-wing positions without jeopardizing his ability to win a general election. The small left-wing magazine Current Affairs asked him to respond the next month, and he said, “I really appreciate the question, because I really want us to step back and ask a couple of very basic points about how politics actually work, not from the Atlantic desk where you have a vested interest in sustaining a system that whitewashes neoliberal ideas and continues to tell us the best use of our money is to subsidize big corporations or a foreign government.” [ Jonathan Chait: What Abdul El-Sayed doesn’t get about Trump ] The “foreign government” he refers to is presumably Israel. El-Sayed was not merely disputing the merits of my beliefs (which he mischaracterized—I have argued against aid to Israel, and I have no idea which big corporations he thinks I wish to subsidize). He accused me of representing a “vested interest” in these policies. His campaign declined to respond to multiple emails requesting clarification as to the nature of this alleged vested interest. The combination of populism and anti-Zionism has introduced a strain of political rhetoric that heretofore has had little place within the Democratic Party. Anybody who has observed the Republican Party in the Trump era, however, would recognize the combination of populist demagoguery and edgelord bullying. Informing your supporters that their problems are the result of a shadowy cabal of billionaire conspirators tends to unleash passions that can be difficult to control. El-Sayed and Trump share a gleeful lack of concern for the consequences. Although the comparison may sound like an insult, it’s one El-Sayed has invited himself. Earlier this year, he held a campaign event with Hasan Piker, a popular streamer and enthusiast for left-wing authoritarian regimes. When reporters questioned his choice of allies, El-Sayed replied , “If perfectly inoffensive won elections, then Donald Trump would never have been President.” Democrats now have to decide whether they think they can win elections this way, and whether they want to.

items.title: The Cities That Said Yes to Drugs
items.description: Photographs by Dana Golan Late last year , I walked roughly a mile from downtown Seattle to the working-class neighborhood of Little Saigon and came upon a montage of human despair. An open-air drug market stretched along the intersection of 12th and Jackson: about 250 people, many smoking fentanyl or bent over in the thrall of the drug, tilting as if mid-fall. Three women lay passed out on the sidewalk, their chests slowly rising and falling, while fellow addicts stepped over them and dealers made sales. Young boys, schoolbags on their backs, stood on a far corner and watched. I walked around the block to the Hoa Mai playground, named for a Vietnamese flower that signifies rebirth. City workers had installed gates to keep drug users away, but at 4 p.m. on a Wednesday, I counted 27 people smoking drugs and nodding off. No children were in sight. Half a mile to the south, in the Beacon Hill neighborhood, I visited a 10-acre park named after the Filipino nationalist Jose Rizal. It has a playground and the remnants of an apple orchard, and at night you can peer downtown and see the city lights. As I arrived, a drug user squatted next to a child’s slide and relieved himself. Others had set up tents and colonized the park pavilion, where they heated fentanyl on tinfoil and inhaled the fumes with glass pipes. A few went old-school and injected it. Across the street, I spoke with Angelina Monsegur as she waited at a bus stop. When she was a kid, she told me, she and her father ate candied apples in the park and watched Fourth of July fireworks. A few weeks earlier, she and her 6-year-old daughter had gotten on the bus and seen a man smoking fentanyl on board. “Are you serious?” she’d shouted at him. “My daughter has asthma.” I asked if she had called the police, and she smiled at my naivete. “All the city does is send out teams who hand out aluminum foil and fentanyl pipes.” Seattle is one of the wealthiest and best-educated cities in the world. It can afford to try various strategies to address its drug epidemic and high rate of fatal overdoses. Yet many of the city’s leaders, apparently supported by voters, view enforcing bans on the open sale and use of narcotics, and forcing addicts off the streets and into treatment, as akin to an act of state repression. Seattle, like a striking number of other liberal American cities, has embraced a radical form of “harm reduction,” which is more a philosophy about treating addiction than a scientific approach to it. Harm reduction’s adherents hold that police and outreach workers should “meet the addicted where they are,” which is to say without judgment. The New York State Department of Health , a bastion of harm reduction, describes it as a “social movement” committed to “building leadership” among drug users. In these places, de facto and sometimes legal restrictions on narcotics use have been greatly loosened; cities fund teams of workers to hand out drug paraphernalia, and in some rare cases they’ve created dedicated spaces for addicts to shoot up. Meanwhile, police departments struggling with staffing shortages and budget cuts have stopped devoting resources to sweeping users and dealers off the streets or out of parks and playgrounds. Harm reduction was born 50 years ago of an admirable humanitarian impulse. Its most basic ideas, such as providing clean needles to users, deservedly draw broad support. There’s a debate to be had, though, about whether this approach has saved lives or added to the carnage of America’s terrible drug epidemic. From 2014 to 2024, roughly 862,000 Americans died of drug overdoses, more than twice the toll of the previous decade. Several studies have shown that addicts who shoot up at official injection sites are far less likely to die of overdoses than those who use drugs in, say, alleyways and parks. Over the past decade, however, overdose-death rates climbed sharply in nearly every city where the strongest harm-reduction policies were in place, and even with declines in the past two years, the rates remain well above those of previous decades. From 2016 to 2025, 7,089 people died of overdoses in King County, which includes Seattle—seven times the number of homicides in that period. Harm reduction isn’t just a problem for addicts. In many cities, the autonomy of drug users has taken precedence over nearly everything and everyone else, not least working-class families like Monsegur’s who must live alongside addicts and accept dystopian decay. Keith Humphreys, a Stanford psychiatry and behavioral-sciences professor and a former adviser to President Obama, supports needle exchanges and opposes the widespread jailing of users. But when he argues that drug policy must take into account the impact on communities, he told me, some critics dismiss him as a reactionary. Their arguments, he said, “sound a lot more like gun rights and vaccine refusal. It’s no longer about the whole population; it’s about the subset who use drugs.” In recent years, officials in cities such as San Francisco and Philadelphia have moved to rein in the excesses of harm-reduction policies. Nevertheless, these policies retain a powerful hold on public-health and political leaders in blue parts of the country. I witnessed this in visits to Seattle and Burlington, Vermont—two of America’s more progressive cities. Both are afflicted by high overdose rates, overwhelmed police forces, parks and public squares often captive to drug use, and the theft and disorder that accompany all of that. Yet many of their elected officials continue to insist, despite everything, that harm reduction is the most effective and moral solution to addiction. Dana Golan for The Atlantic In Seattle’s working-class Little Saigon neighborhood, where hundreds of people gather in open-air drug markets, businesses and playgrounds have installed gates to keep addicts away. Harm reduction took root in the 1970s in the Netherlands, where addicts formed unions—the Junkiebond in Rotterdam, for instance—that distributed needles and pushed back against official insistence on abstinence from hard drugs. Not long afterward, this philosophy gained support in some American and Canadian cities. I first encountered it when I reported on a heroin-shooting gallery in Bushwick, Brooklyn, in 1991. The work of harm-reduction advocates at the time undoubtedly saved lives. HIV-infection rates for drug users in Bushwick had reached 50 percent or higher, at a time when that diagnosis was close to a death sentence. Activists risked arrest to distribute clean needles and bleach to disinfect used ones. But some began to argue for a more radical step: There would be less death, they said, if addicts could inject drugs without fear of arrest. That momentous step came about not in New York but in Vancouver, a city whose political culture was left-wing and libertarian, celebrating the rights of the individual. In 2003, as overdose deaths surged, the Liberal Party of Canada carved out an exemption to federal drug laws and established North America’s first sanctioned injection site, in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside, a troubled dockside neighborhood. Addicts could bring their heroin and cocaine to a 13-seat center where staff dispensed needles, swabs, and sterile water to cook the drugs and offered advice on vein maintenance. Clinic staff were trained to reverse overdoses, and if that failed, to call a hospital for help. Initial opinion surveys found broad public support for the center, and it shone like a beacon for some activists, academics, and journalists in the United States and other parts of Canada. A stream of studies and articles celebrated Vancouver’s legal shooting gallery , which resulted in fewer cases of AIDS and other infections, and fewer deaths. Public-health officials coined a nonjudgmental nomenclature that persists to this day. The word addict was stigmatizing; better to refer to people who use drugs . People used rather than abused narcotics. They did not fail a drug test ; they tested positive . Vancouver’s model spawned dozens of injection sites across Canada. Health officials in British Columbia went still further, championing a program known as “safer supply”: Former government officials started companies that provided addicts with free opioid alternatives such as pharmaceutical-grade hydromorphone pills—considerably more powerful than heroin. Drug users obtained these pills from pharmacies and specially designed vending machines. By 2020, the rights of addicts in the province had edged toward the fantastical. In 2023, the province decriminalized small amounts of certain hard drugs. One hospital instructed nurses not to confiscate fentanyl or meth from patients and not to restrict suspected dealers from visiting patients. When British Columbia banned illicit-drug use within 50 feet of a public park, playground, or swimming pool, the provincial supreme court blocked the law, ruling that it could cause “irreparable harm” to drug users. “Harm reductionists had the force of a bulldozer,” Julian Somers, who studies addiction at Simon Fraser University, told me. Some addicts learned to game the system by obtaining daily allotments of hydromorphone pills—15 or more a day was typical—and then selling them to dealers in exchange for stronger fentanyl concoctions. Dealers could then sell the original pills on the street. An investigation by the National Post reported a price drop of 70 percent or more for black-market pills in cities that had instituted safer supply. This, in turn, expanded the circle of the addicted and led to more overdoses. Gary Coronado / Los Angeles Times / Getty Medics attend to a man who overdosed on drugs in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside neighborhood. Thousands of addicts have poured into the city since it opened North America’s first sanctioned injection site, inspiring similar programs across the U.S. and Canada. The consequences were predictable. Over the course of two decades, many thousands of drug users poured into the Downtown Eastside and other Canadian neighborhoods in search of narcotics and places to shoot up. Overdoses spiked. In 2014, British Columbia recorded 369 overdose deaths; in 2023, the figure peaked at more than 2,500. Fatal overdoses last year decreased to 1,826, as Canada moved to reverse decriminalization and tighten regulation of narcotics, but that still represents a nearly ninefold increase over 15 years. Advocates of harm reduction have long held that more addicts would die if officials closed injection centers. But a recent study found that after an injection site in Alberta closed, there was no increase in the number of overdose deaths, and more addicts sought treatment. Advocates have also insisted that crime does not spike near injection centers, but the data are more mixed than they admit. Not long ago, I walked through a park in Toronto to a fence with hundreds of purple ribbons tied to it. Each represented a resident who had died of an overdose, and I was unavoidably moved. Then, as I read a leaflet, I realized that the memorial was the work of the Harm Reduction Advocacy Collective, “a liberation movement of people who use drugs,” along with public-health professionals and academics who “stand up for the rights of drug users.” It’s one of a number of similar groups in Canada, such as the Substance Use Health Network , which condemns “anti-euphoria prohibitionist principles” such as “the idea that illicit drugs are inherently bad.” British Columbia is starting to rethink its runaway experiment. In 2025, the province began requiring addicts using the safer-supply program to consume their prescribed narcotics in front of pharmacists, and earlier this year, the drug-decriminalization program expired. Provincial health authorities are now making attempts to encourage addicts to get treatment. The sense is of a political culture reluctantly shaking off a decades-long stupor. In 2024, the premier of British Columbia appointed Daniel Vigo, a psychiatrist and public-health researcher, as the province’s chief scientific adviser on toxic drugs. Vigo has spoken of the terrible toll that repeat overdoses take on addicts’ brains, and has advocated for a new policy of mandating treatment for some addicts. Progressive activists and journalists tend to talk about forced treatment as a conservative-driven return to a carceral state, but considerable data show that addicts who enter mandated treatment are as likely to avoid drug use and rearrest as the relatively small number who seek treatment voluntarily. Vigo’s words today would have amounted to heresy a few years ago. “It’s as if we forgot that the goal was to try and stop people from getting addicted,” he told me, adding later: “Harm reduction gets people in trouble when it stops being one part of a holistic strategy and it becomes an ideological movement.” But even as Vancouver has begun the painful process of revising its harm-reduction policies, the city still exerts a powerful hold on the imagination of liberal leaders in the United States. In New York City, which established two injection sites in 2021, health officials and academics point to the perceived success of Vancouver as inspiration. Rhode Island, where an injection center opened in Providence in 2024, also holds up Vancouver as a model. The Washington State legislature appointed a working group that in 2025 recommended establishing a safe supply of narcotics for addicts, and officials repeatedly cited the Vancouver program. The shadow cast by Vancouver extends to Burlington. Last year, the city council approved the establishment of an injection center. The group that the city chose to run it noted that Vancouver “remains the source of much of the evidence” showing the benefits of such spaces for drug users and the community. Burlington sits on Lake Champlain, the Adirondack Mountains rising on the far shore. It’s a beautiful city, but its drug scene is not covert, spreading over downtown and several other neighborhoods. Users pitch tents in churchyards and parks and along the waterfront. When I sat in City Hall Park last September, I counted at least 70 users and dealers, many looking hyperkinetic in the way of the strung out. I walked through an alley next to city hall where, a few weeks earlier, a group of young people had allegedly beaten a man to death in an argument over drugs. Vermont has strict laws against possession of heroin and cocaine, but users in Burlington are rarely arrested or prosecuted for possessing small amounts. Although it’s hard to isolate the effects of these policies, in 2024, the city of almost 45,000 recorded 585 drug overdoses, 28 of which were fatal. That is more than twice the rate of fatal overdoses per capita in New York City the same year. Beth Sightler walked me around her working-class neighborhood in the Old North End. Burlington’s progressive political culture and tradition of caring for the poor are well established; Bernie Sanders served four terms as mayor in the 1980s. Sightler, a liberal who runs a mental-health center, said she has fished needles out of her flower boxes and seen people overdosing in cars and cemeteries. She carries naloxone, a medication that can reverse an opioid overdose, when she walks her dog. One morning she saw a young woman on the grass near her porch wearing underwear, a bra, and sandals. “There was this beautiful woman, absolutely beautiful, sitting there trying to find a vein and inject,” Sightler recalled. “I told her, ‘Sweetie, you gotta move along.’” Many people in Burlington offer similar stories. A block from City Hall Park, the King Street Center provides tutoring and recreation programs for families living in poverty. Staff members arrive early to sweep up needles outside the building. When drug dealers began playing dice out front last summer, Shabnam Nolan, the executive director, called the police, who eventually chased the dealers away. “We’ve tried to sound the alarm, and yet people are not taking us seriously enough about what’s happening,” Nolan told me. Why does a drug user’s “right to ‘dignity’ violate children’s right to come to our center without seeing blood and needles?” “It’s as if,” she said of Burlington and its culture, “we are frozen with fear that someone might see us as uncompassionate.” The city’s political class has compounded these problems. In 2020, activists launched a campaign to defund the police department, although it was regarded as relatively progressive and community-oriented. The city council cut almost $1 million from the police budget. Six years ago, Burlington had about 100 officers; now it has fewer than 70. The current city-council president, Ben Traverse, a liberal Democrat who has grown uncomfortable with Burlington’s direction, told me that sometimes as few as five officers are on duty citywide after midnight on the weekends. It used to be that if you wanted to deal drugs, “you did not come to Burlington,” Traverse said. But that’s changed: “Open-air drug sales are a common occurrence here.” State’s Attorney Sarah George, the prosecutor for the county that includes Burlington, is a progressive Democrat who once wrote that the American legal system “was built on the oppression and caging of black, brown, and poor people.” She told me that the combination of COVID, ever less affordable housing, and a cascade of evictions fed a drug crisis that has devastated Vermont. But she doesn’t blame addicts, who she said are “rarely dangerous” and are suffering. “I’m very frustrated with this narrative that City Hall Park is the end of the world,” George added. “That park is still a very safe place to be.” I asked her how Burlington might balance drug users’ sometimes dominant presence in the city’s parks and streets with the desire of residents to use and enjoy those same places. The city, she replied, should start by opening its planned injection center so that addicts can use drugs in private. The state legislature has allocated about $2 million that it obtained from a national opioid settlement to help fund the center, though potential neighbors have pushed back against the sites that have been floated so far. More broadly, George opposes pushing addicts to the margins. “They cannot be disappeared,” she said. “They are part of our community.” In 2022, George announced a new policy: If police officers stopped cars with broken taillights, tinted windows, or expired licenses and found a cache of narcotics, her office would most likely decline to prosecute the cases, on the grounds that racial discrimination could have motivated the traffic stops. She emphasized to me that police officers could in any case confiscate and destroy the drugs. But she questioned the need to go beyond that. “Is prosecution needed?” she said. “Or have we done enough already?” George has been reelected twice and is running for a third term. In April, I spoke with Burlington’s mayor, Emma Mulvaney-Stanak, of the Vermont Progressive Party, which has governed the city for much of the past four decades. She has seen firsthand the effects of the drug epidemic. When she lived in the Old North End and her child was a toddler, they awoke to drug dealers beating on their door. She told me that she supports police and Drug Enforcement Administration investigations that target dealers, although she noted the “whack-a-mole” nature of that work, as new dealers replace those who are arrested. She said that without more help from the county and state, the city lacks the funds to build larger shelters that could help keep addicts off the streets. She is aware that Burlingtonians have grown impatient living with a drug-abuse epidemic. “We are fatigued with our compassion,” she told me. “All of the attention on harm reduction and public health—I get that.” But, like George, Mulvaney-Stanak has not backed away from harm-reduction policies that she sees as humane and essential. Last summer, she opposed a city-council resolution calling for police officers to be stationed in City Hall Park to clear out users and dealers, arguing that the drug traffic would only go elsewhere and that there were not enough officers to enforce the policy. She signed off on the resolution, but she shares George’s philosophical objections: “Displacement and removal of people is not the solution,” the mayor said. Wouldn’t an injection center, I asked her, draw more addicts and dealers to Burlington? She acknowledged the possibility, but framed it as a necessary risk. She repeated the harm-reduction maxim: “It helps people where they are at.” The city’s problems, Mulvaney-Stanak insisted, were more image than reality: “People need to ignore the clickbaity articles that distort the nature of Burlington.” Recently, Traverse and other Democrats on the city council have begun to challenge the mayor on harm reduction. Jennifer Morrison, the state’s public-safety commissioner, has also spoken up. She served as Burlington’s interim police chief for six months in 2020 before quitting, in part because of what she described as the city’s “mismanagement” and “social activism.” She and Governor Phil Scott, a moderate Republican, have clashed with Mulvaney-Stanak. They have periodically, at the city’s request, sent state troopers to Burlington to help local police with drug enforcement and patrolling the central business district. “I lived through the decisions that got us to the place that we are now,” Morrison told me. “We are exposing our youth to terrible consequences by normalizing drug use and addiction.” The business community in Burlington has also pushed back. In more than a dozen interviews, local merchants spoke of feeling abandoned. In testimony before the state legislature, the owner of Outdoor Gear Exchange reported that in 2024, the business lost an estimated $400,000 to shoplifting, as addicts stole to support their habit. At Homeport, a 40-year-old home-furnishings store downtown, a co-owner, Mark Bouchett, told me that he lost $95,000 to shoplifting in 2024 and was forced to hire a security guard. Drug users defecate in the doorways of businesses. Bouchett joined 170 other business owners and restaurateurs who last year wrote an open letter to the mayor warning that the city was in crisis. Their tone was reasonable; they sought treatment for addicts, not incarceration. But a broad coalition of the political left in Burlington—unions, harm-reduction groups, pro-Palestine and trans-rights activist groups, and the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America—countered with their own letter, in which they denounced the business owners and demanded that they open bathrooms and sheltered doorways to addicts. To call for more police to help address the city’s drug problem, this group wrote, would “further harm our most vulnerable community members.” One of the signatories, Food Not Cops Burlington, posted and then deleted a boycott map targeting the business owners. Overdose deaths in Vermont dropped last year to 170, a 37 percent decrease from the peak in 2022, but still far above the 78 deaths recorded in 2010. At the Ben & Jerry’s on Church Street, I saw staff hand out cards to customers who asked to use the bathroom: “Vermont is experiencing a tragic increase in overdose fatalities. Our bathroom has also become a destination for folks seeking to inject drugs.” The bathroom was permanently locked. Families and children speak of being left on their own to navigate these harsh realities. Through the King Street Center, I met a young woman who was earning top grades at the University of Vermont. When she walks her younger sisters home from school, they pass drug dealers on the way. A Burlington High School student told me that her teachers have instructed students to avoid eye contact with dealers and users. A week earlier, she said, an addict had trailed her home after volleyball practice. She broke into a run, yelling for help, and the person eventually turned away. Then there was Britany, a mother of three young children, who moved two years ago from a homeless shelter to an apartment on King Street. (She asked me not to use her last name, fearing for her family’s safety.) She said that she often found drug paraphernalia in the apartment building and, on some nights, encountered an addict sleeping in the hallway; her next-door neighbor was a fentanyl dealer. She had constructed a safe room for her children to flee to in case of gunfire. “Everyone talks about needle exchange and harm reduction,” she said. “I mean, okay. But it’s like my children and I are living in the zombie apocalypse.” Just a few years ago, voters in Seattle seemed primed for a change. In 2021, they elected Ann Davison, a moderate and independent-minded Republican, as city attorney. Sara Nelson, a Democrat who had advertised her willingness to challenge the harm-reduction consensus, won a seat on the city council the same year and became its president two years later. With support from Davison, she passed laws cracking down on open drug use, prostitution, and dealing downtown, and substantially increasing the number of surveillance cameras in high-crime neighborhoods. Nelson persuaded the city council to redirect money to on-demand addiction treatment. “You can’t meet people where they’re at, because where they’re at is on death’s door,” she told me, adding that she believes many addicts can be saved only by a firm push toward treatment. Dana Golan for The Atlantic An encampment in South Queen Anne, Seattle. Since taking office in January, Mayor Katie Wilson has authorized sweeps of encampments and signaled an openness to pulling back on harm-reduction policies. Nelson also asked pointed questions about what had become the received wisdom in Seattle, such as why the county government paid millions of dollars to supply kits to addicts with tinfoil, pipes, and instructions on how to smoke fentanyl. (Incongruously, these kits came emblazoned with an image of Martin Luther King Jr., the namesake of King County.) What harm was reduced, Nelson asked at a 2023 council hearing, by helping addicts get high? Amber Tejada, an employee of a health nonprofit that had partnered with the city, raised her hand to answer. “I know it can be a little controversial,” she told the councilwoman, “but one of the key tenets of harm reduction that I see is that we want to be able to facilitate and champion autonomy of people who use drugs.” Tejada added, “There are folks for whom abstinence is not something by which they measure their success in life.” Nelson was no hard-line conservative. She pushed to expand the number of treatment beds for addicts and talked openly of her own past struggles with alcohol. But in elections last November, voters turned out both her and Davison. Their replacements had concerns over the use of surveillance cameras and opposed laws that barred repeat public drug users from certain areas in the city. I spoke with Davison in her office shortly before her term was up. She wrestled with her sense of a job not completed. “It’s really sad to watch the slow death of so many people,” she said, adding later, “You cannot act like this is a victimless crime.” [ Read: Crime in Chicago is a choice ] I asked Sandeep Kaushik, a Democratic political consultant who has lived in Seattle for decades, if he could explain the persistent attraction of radical harm-reduction policies in his city. Kaushik described himself as an “unreconstructed Obama Democrat,” which he noted “codes me as a conservative in some circles here.” He told me that local leaders “really believe the city should be on the leading edge of translating progressive ideas into policy.” There is also a curious disconnect between the policies that political leaders put in place and the desires of voters. In many polls, Seattle residents list crime and illegal drug use as among their greatest concerns, and a Seattle Times survey three years ago found that 60 percent of respondents wanted police to arrest those who used drugs in public places. Last year, the city elected a new mayor, Katie Wilson, a self-described democratic socialist with no experience in elected office. Wilson has signaled an openness to pulling back some harm-reduction policies. Before she officially entered the race, she wrote an essay for Seattle’s alt-weekly , The Stranger , in which she cautioned fellow leftists against smugness. “The central weakness of the left narrative,” she wrote, “is a habit of deflection that makes it sound, at best, as though we are in denial about the grim reality on the streets.” The left, she continued, should not trivialize “what anyone who spends some time walking around Seattle’s streets can plainly observe: People with acute mental illness whose behavior is disturbed and occasionally aggressive. People using drugs, often incapacitated or passed out on the ground.” Since she took office, Wilson has backed up her words by signing off on sweeps of large encampments in parks. Police and city workers have dismantled tents and carted away garbage. In late June, the mayor emerged from what she described in a statement as a period of “deep listening” and promised to “disrupt the drug dealing” and “public disorder” that plague the city’s Little Saigon and Beacon Hill neighborhoods. The police, she said, would commit more officers to those areas, and arrest users and dealers or press them to accept treatment. For a Seattle politician to argue that tolerating drug crime and disorder amounts to harm enhancement registered as something close to startling news. Yet Wilson runs a political risk. By pledging to crack down, she has broken with many of her allies and supporters. Now she will be judged by her ability to clear the city’s streets. Andrea Suarez leads a group, We Heart Seattle, that combines care for the homeless with a hardheaded insistence on legal consequences and addiction treatment for drug users. She was in Jose Rizal Park when police swept it one day in April, and watched users and dealers amble off into the woods or walk over to Little Saigon. They returned a few hours later, she told me. A day or two after that, the tents reappeared. “Everyone who lives in this park knows there is no consequence for being swept multiple times or doing drugs or vandalizing a park,” Suarez said. Dana Golan for The Atlantic People who live in Jose Rizal Park know “there is no consequence for being swept multiple times or doing drugs or vandalizing a park,” one community activist says. What’s baffling is that none of this lies beyond the ability of city officials to address. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie has instructed police to crack down on dealers and dismantle tent cities. Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker has sent officers into drug-scarred neighborhoods and established a treatment court, which offers first-time felony drug offenders a chance to avoid jail if they enter a treatment program. San Jose, California, has put more police officers in targeted neighborhoods, built emergency housing as police dismantle homeless encampments, and increased fines for landlords whose abandoned buildings are used by dealers to sell drugs and guns. In Boston, Mayor Michelle Wu was once enamored of harm reduction and injection centers. But she has ordered police to clear street encampments, and her administration now puts more emphasis on pushing addicts into treatment, by detaining them if necessary. Wu has also dropped all mention of injection centers from her plans. In Seattle, by contrast, efforts to reduce public drug use force afflicted neighborhoods to pay a high price. For years, when playgrounds and parks became drug hot spots, the city reacted by fencing them off, depriving families of access. In May, police and city workers returned to Jose Rizal Park and again booted out dealers and addicts, preparing the park for a renovation. As a first step, city workers dismantled the picnic pavilion where addicts smoked and shot up, its condition having deteriorated from all the misuse. Park officials do not plan on replacing it, acknowledging the obvious in bureaucratese: The park “has been impacted by activities not aligned with intended use.” The bus shelter around the corner, where drug users gathered day and night, was also ripped out “because of an increase in loitering, littering and vandalism,” a King County Metro representative told me by email. All of this felt like another admission of defeat—officials destroying Seattle in the name of saving it. This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “The Cities That Said Yes to Drugs.”

items.title: Session extraordinaire du Parlement : le président Doumbouya convoque les députés à partir du 3 août
items.description: Le président Mamadi Doumbouya, a signé un décret convoquant l'Assemblée nationale en session extraordinaire à compter du vendredi 3 août 2026 à 10 heures. Le texte, diffusé ce 29 juillet 2026 à la télévision nationale, vise à assurer la continuité de l'action législative pendant la période des vacances parlementaires. Selon le décret, cette convocation intervient conformément aux dispositions des articles 96 et 97 de la Constitution du 26 septembre 2025, ainsi qu'à l'article 68 de la loi organique portant règlement intérieur de l'Assemblée nationale. Le décret précise également qu'elle fait suite à une demande du bureau de l'institution parlementaire. L'ordre du jour de cette session extraordinaire est limité à des questions bien précises. Les députés auront notamment à examiner et ratifier les ordonnances transmises par le gouvernement. Ils devront également se prononcer sur un projet de loi d'habilitation autorisant le président de la République à prendre, par ordonnance, des mesures relevant du domaine de la loi pendant les vacances parlementaires. Cette habilitation couvrira la période allant de l'adoption de ladite loi jusqu'au 5 octobre 2026. Le décret rappelle par ailleurs que, conformément à l'article 68 du règlement intérieur de l'Assemblée nationale, cette session extraordinaire prendra fin dès l'épuisement de l'ordre du jour fixé.

items.title: Guinée : la HAC lève les sanctions contre trois journalistes
items.description: La Haute Autorité de la Communication (HAC) a décidé de lever les sanctions infligées à trois journalistes guinéens et de les autoriser à reprendre immédiatement l'exercice de leur profession. Cette décision, adoptée en séance plénière le 29 juillet 2026, concerne Mamadi Konoma Keïta, journaliste basé à Mandiana, Ibrahima Diakité, journaliste à Dinguiraye, ainsi que Saïfoulaye Diallo, correspondant régional de l'Agence guinéenne de presse (AGP) à Labé. Selon la décision n°029/HAC/2026, cette mesure de clémence fait suite aux demandes de pardon formulées par les trois journalistes, aux regrets qu'ils ont exprimés ainsi qu'à leurs engagements écrits à respecter les lois, les règles déontologiques et le cadre réglementaire régissant l'exploitation des médias en Guinée. Le Collège de la HAC précise également avoir pris en considération les nombreuses démarches de médiation ainsi que les appels à la clémence émanant d'autorités religieuses, de sages, d'organisations professionnelles des médias et de plusieurs personnalités originaires de Mandiana, Dinguiraye et Labé. Dans sa décision, l'institution annonce officiellement la levée de l'interdiction d'exercer qui frappait les trois professionnels des médias. « L'interdiction d'exercer la profession de journaliste pesant sur Messieurs Mamadi Konoma Keïta, Ibrahima Diakité et Saïfoulaye Diallo est entièrement levée à compter de la date de signature de la présente décision. Les intéressés sont officiellement autorisés à reprendre toutes leurs activités professionnelles », indique la HAC. L'autorité de régulation annonce également la levée de la suspension et de l'interdiction de diffusion visant les médias dont ces journalistes sont promoteurs, sous réserve de leur mise en conformité administrative immédiate auprès des services techniques compétents de la HAC. « La suspension et l'interdiction de diffusion qui frappaient les médias dont ils sont les promoteurs sont levées, sous réserve de la mise en conformité administrative immédiate de leurs cahiers des charges auprès des services techniques compétents de la HAC », précise la décision. Par ailleurs, la carte de presse professionnelle d'Ibrahima Diakité lui est officiellement restituée. Toutefois, la Haute Autorité de la Communication souligne que cette mesure de clémence ne constitue en aucun cas un précédent. Elle met en garde les bénéficiaires contre toute récidive ou tout nouveau manquement aux règles de la profession. « La HAC avertit que toute récidive ou manquement futur aux règles d'éthique, de déontologie, de préservation de l'ordre public et de respect du vivre-ensemble entraînera l'application immédiate et irrévocable des sanctions maximales prévues par les textes en vigueur », prévient l'institution. Signée par le président de la HAC, Boubacar Yacine Diallo, cette décision met fin aux sanctions administratives prononcées contre les trois journalistes, tout en réaffirmant les exigences de responsabilité, de professionnalisme et de respect des règles qui encadrent l'exercice du métier de journaliste en Guinée.

items.title: Canicule en Tunisie : les hôpitaux sous pression, l’état d’urgence réclamé
items.description: En Tunisie , qui est la principale destination des touristes algériens en été, les syndicats de la santé tirent la sonnette d’alarme. Face à la canicule qui frappe le pays et les coupures d’électricité, ils appellent à décréter l’état d’urgence. Dans un communiqué commun publié mercredi, quatre organisations syndicales ont saisi le ministère de la Santé pour lui demander de prendre des mesures d’urgence afin de « préserver le fonctionnement des hôpitaux publics et de protéger les patients ». Pour ces syndicats, la canicule et les coupures d’électricité pèsent lourdement sur les « capacités des établissements hospitaliers et met sous pression les professionnels de santé », selon le site Webdo. Si les services de maternité n’ont pas été affectés jusque-là par les coupures d’électricité grâce aux groupes électrogènes, les syndicats de la santé tunisiens alertent sur un « risque croissant sur l’ensemble du système de santé ». Autrement dit, des incidents peuvent se produire et mettre en danger la prise en charge des nouveau-nées et des accouchements dans les hôpitaux tunisiens. Canicule en Tunisie : les syndicats de la santé alertent sur les risques Face à cette situation, les représentants des soignants appellent le ministère de la Santé à décréter « l’état d’urgence sanitaire et à activer des cellules de crise aussi bien au niveau central qu’au sein des hôpitaux publics », selon la même source. Ils réclament la mise en place d’un « protocole national unifié » pour la prévention et la prise en charge des maladies liées à la canicule. Ils revendiquent aussi des « moyens financiers exceptionnels » aux hôpitaux publics afin de leur permettre d’assurer leurs missions dans des « conditions particulièrement difficiles ». La Tunisie a fait face ces derniers jours à une vague de chaleur exceptionnelle avec des températures frôlant les 50°C, ce qui a provoqué des coupures répétitives d’électricité dans tout le pays. L’article Canicule en Tunisie : les hôpitaux sous pression, l'état d'urgence réclamé est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: 11 killed, 6 injured as three-storey house collapses in Lahore's Harbanspura
items.description: LAHORE: Eleven people were killed and six injured after a three-storey house collapsed in Lahore’s Harbanspura late on Wednesday, according to authorities. Spokesperson for the Lahore deputy commissioner Harris Ali confirmed to Dawn that the death toll of the incident had risen to 11 after rescue workers pulled out the body of a minor girl. The rescue operation ended following the recovery of the girl’s body, he said. The spokesperson said three brothers and their families were residing in the building, and they were joined by their sister and her children for a birthday celebration on Wednesday night, following which the structure collapsed. “The building collapsed floor by floor from the top down,” he said. The cause of the collapse is yet to be determined, for which Lahore DC retired Capt Muhammad Ali Ijaz has ordered an inquiry, a statement issued by his office said. The statement said he supervised the rescue operation, adding that Rescue 1122 teams, assisted by district administration officials, carried out the operation. Heavy machinery had also been deployed to speed up the operation, it said. The incident comes a month after a roof collapse at a tuition centre in Lahore’s Kahna area claimed the lives of 14 children. Police had registered a case against the tuition centre’s owners and the building’s contractor a day after the incident, with the first information report stating that the suspects were putting soil on the dilapidated building’s roof, which collapsed because of the extra load. In a similar incident in early May, four children were killed and 20 people injured after the roof of a classroom at a private school in Dera Ghazi Khan collapsed. A probe into the incident revealed that construction for an extension of the building was under way when the roof of the classroom collapsed. According to the district administration’s incident report, the roof was overloaded as sand and bricks were placed on it, and it could not bear the load and consequently collapsed.
